rows.scope: Hours that recreational boats, registered and unregistered, were operated out on the water in calendar 2018, all 50 states and DC, estimated by the 2018 NRBSS Exposure Survey, run monthly by RTI International for the Coast Guard: 213,659 addresses sampled, 44,422 surveys returned, 31,733 from boat-owning households; a registry frame (commercial list of registered boats) plus an address-based sample for households with only unregistered boats; eight states barred registry sharing. 'Boat hours' is the hours a boat is used out on the water in a period (p. 4). Boat-hours, not person-hours.
rows.source: U.S. Coast Guard, bulletin 'U.S. Coast Guard releases National Recreational Boating Safety Survey results' (7 Dec 2020), releasing the 2018 NRBSS Exposure Survey Final Report (RTI International, October 2020 (file dated 30 Nov 2020))
rows.do_not_add_to: An exposure denominator, not a count of people or deaths: never added to any deaths row. Not paired with uscg-boating-2024 or us-location-boating-2024 (2024 deaths against 2018 hours) and not added to or averaged with us-nrbss-person-hours-2012 (person-hours, 2012). Any risk ratio built on it must name the 2018 fatality count and state the rule used.
rows.note: Graded C on verification: the only primary-publisher document reached that prints 3.42 billion is the Coast Guard's own release bulletin; the report's Table 3-36 (p. 66) was not read (text extraction stops at p. 18). Regrade A once a person confirms Table 3-36 by eye. The same release prints 25.4 million boats owned, 13.4 million unregistered. Same population as the Coast Guard's boating deaths series, but the years differ (2018 against 2024); the next survey is 2026.

rows.figure: 84,544 thousand persons (26.5% of the U.S. population)
rows.scope: Persons who went out on the water aboard a recreational boat at least once in 2018 ('boater', report p. 14), all ages, United States, estimated from the NRBSS Participation Survey: address-based household sample fielded in four quarterly waves during 2018 by RTI International for the Coast Guard; 43,590 addresses sampled, 5,851 completed responses, 14.9% response rate. The same table gives 28.37 million households (23.3%) with at least one boater.
rows.source: U.S. Coast Guard, 2018 National Recreational Boating Safety Survey, Participation Survey Final Report (RTI International, October 2020 (file dated 30 Nov 2020)), Table 3-1, p. 14
rows.do_not_add_to: A participation head-count, not a trip or hour count and not a deaths row: never added to any US drowning count; not divided into us-nrbss-boat-hours-2018 to make hours per boater (the Coast Guard did not print that). The release rounds it to '84.5 million Americans'.
rows.note: Participation (persons) is the loosest exposure unit: one boater may boat once or two hundred times. The same report's Section 3.4 gives days per boater (us-nrbss-boating-days-per-boater-2018).

rows.scope: Mean number of boating days per boater in 2018, where a boating day is 'any day that a person spent some time out on the water on a recreational boat' (report Section 3.4, p. 19); median 8.0 days; persons in boat-owning households averaged about 25.8 days (Table 3-10, p. 24). Survey as in us-nrbss-boaters-2018. National totals of boat days, person boat days and person boat hours are in the separate Exposure Survey report (Tables 3-24, 3-28, 3-44, 3-46), which could not be read past p. 18 here.
rows.source: U.S. Coast Guard, 2018 National Recreational Boating Safety Survey, Participation Survey Final Report (RTI International, October 2020 (file dated 30 Nov 2020)), Section 3.4 and Table 3-6, p. 19
rows.do_not_add_to: A per-person mean: not multiplied by us-nrbss-boaters-2018 to make a person-days total (that total exists in the Exposure report and should be read there), and never added to any deaths row.
rows.note: Exposure in days, not hours: a day on the water counts whether it lasted ten minutes or ten hours.

rows.scope: Estimated hours persons spent on board recreational boats taken out on the water in 2012, United States, from the 2012 NRBSS, as restated in the introduction (p. 1) of the 2018 NRBSS Exposure Survey Final Report; the same page says boats were out on the water an average of about 11.3 days and 4.5 hours per day in 2012, and that 22,217,000 registered and unregistered recreational boats were owned, about 55% registered and about 66% operated at least once.
rows.source: U.S. Coast Guard, 2018 National Recreational Boating Safety Survey, Exposure Survey Final Report (RTI International, October 2020 (file dated 30 Nov 2020), v3.0), Section 1, p. 1, restating the 2012 survey
rows.do_not_add_to: A 2012 figure in person-hours: not added to or averaged with us-nrbss-boat-hours-2018 (boat-hours, 2018) and not paired with any deaths year other than 2012. The 2012 survey report itself was not opened.
rows.note: Recorded because it is the only national person-hours total that could be read from a Coast Guard document here; the 2018 person-hours total exists in the same report's Table 3-46 but was not reachable.

rows.figure: boating deaths in states per 100 million exposure hours ranged from 3 to 130
rows.scope: Range across states of recreational boating deaths per 100 million exposure hours, 2011 data, as printed in the Exposure Survey report's Section 1.2 (Risk Ratios, pp. 4-5) to show why exposure denominators matter; two states are contrasted at 121 and 82 deaths per 100 million exposure hours. The states are not named in the portion read, and the report's own tables behind the range were not reached.
rows.source: U.S. Coast Guard, 2018 National Recreational Boating Safety Survey, Exposure Survey Final Report (RTI International, October 2020 (file dated 30 Nov 2020), v3.0), Section 1.2, pp. 4-5
rows.do_not_add_to: A range of state rates, not a national rate: never averaged, never applied to another year, and never set beside resident-based rates such as us-total-2022 as if comparable. The errata (28 Oct 2022) rewrites the surrounding text so that exposure is the denominator and casualties the numerator.
rows.note: The clearest proof that a risk per exposure has been published for boating. Section 3.22 (pp. 91-109) of the same report prints 2018 state risk ratios per 100 million boat days and per million boat hours (the errata corrects the Maine entry to 56 per 100 million boat days and 10 per million boat hours) but was not readable here.

rows.scope: Estimated beach attendance for 2023 as of 4 Nov 2023, compiled by USLA from the reports of its affiliated lifeguard agencies ('Nationwide Incident Data' table, p. 2); typically more than 140 agencies/beaches report each year; not all US beaches contribute, and the method agencies use to estimate attendance is not described. Same table: 64,578 rescues, 104 drownings in unguarded areas, 16 in guarded areas.
rows.source: United States Lifesaving Association, Board of Directors report 'Statistics Activity' (Feb 2024), p. 2, 2023 National Lifesaving Statistics
rows.do_not_add_to: Attendance at reporting USLA agencies only, a partial-year snapshot: not a count of US beach visits, not added across years or to the Australian visitation rows, and never used as a denominator for CDC or WHO death counts. It pairs only with the drownings in the same table (usla-drownings-guarded-2023), which is what USLA itself does.
rows.note: This is the kind of denominator behind usla-guarded-risk (1 in 18 million over ten years). The per-year series lives in the USLA statistics database (arc.usla.org), which refused automated fetching. Brewster, Gould and Brander (2019) note the dataset cannot be shown to represent proportional exposure per visitor.

rows.scope: Fatal drownings reported by USLA-affiliated agencies for 2023 as of 4 Nov 2023, split by whether they occurred in guarded areas (16) or unguarded areas (104) within reporting agencies' jurisdictions; same table and caveats as usla-beach-attendance-2023. Not vital statistics; not all beaches report; partial year.
rows.source: United States Lifesaving Association, Board of Directors report 'Statistics Activity' (Feb 2024), p. 2, 2023 National Lifesaving Statistics
rows.do_not_add_to: A subset of US drownings with its own case-finding: never added to us-cdc-4500, us-cdc-4345, us-total-2022, uscg-boating-2024 or any WHO/IHME figure. The table prints 16 and 104 separately; no total is formed here. Only the guarded 16 share a denominator with the attendance figure.
rows.note: Recorded so the exposure row has its numerator from the same source, year and beaches. Rescues in the same table: 64,578.

rows.figure: over 500 million individual visitations to the coast
rows.scope: SLSA's estimate of coastal visits by Australian adults (16 and over) in the 12 months before the 2021 National Coastal Safety Survey, derived by SLSA from 14.4 million adults visiting on average 3.3 times each month, with an average 2.3 hours per visit; a visit is any trip to the coast whether or not the person entered the water (activity participants were 10.9 million; swimming/wading 48%, boating 15%, land-based fishing 13%). Financial year 2020/21; a 2% increase on the previous period. Children under 16 are not covered.
rows.source: Surf Life Saving Australia, National Coastal Safety Report 2021, pp. 1 and 7 (read from a copy of the SLSA PDF hosted at marinebusinessnews.com.au; the SLSA original is on Issuu)
rows.do_not_add_to: A survey-based visit estimate for adults: not added to the NSW rows (nsw-coastal-visits-2022-23 is a different year and NSW is inside the national figure) or to usla-beach-attendance-2023; not used as a denominator for australia-2024-25 or australia-location-2024-25 (different years; deaths include children and all coastal activities). SLSA prints its drowning rate per 100,000 population only (0.53 for 2020/21, p. 35).
rows.note: Same report, pp. 1 and 33: 136 coastal drowning deaths in 2020/21 among 241 coastal deaths. SLSA does not divide deaths by visits. Lab judgment (D): a crude risk per coastal visit could be formed from this one report but would set adult visits, many with no water entry, against all-age deaths from every coastal activity; not computed here.

rows.figure: 14.4 million Australian adults (16 years and above) visited the coast
rows.scope: Adults aged 16 and over who visited the coast in the 12 months before the 2021 National Coastal Safety Survey (SLSA's annual survey of coastal participation, behaviours and perceptions; sample size and fieldwork dates are not stated in the portion read). State figures printed on pp. 6-7: NSW 4.7M, QLD 3.1M, VIC 3.4M, WA 1.6M, SA 1.0M, TAS 0.4M, NT 0.2M.
rows.source: Surf Life Saving Australia, National Coastal Safety Report 2021, pp. 5 and 7 (read from a copy of the SLSA PDF hosted at marinebusinessnews.com.au)
rows.do_not_add_to: A head-count of visitors: the state figures are the report's own split and are not re-added here; not added to australia-coastal-visits-2020-21 (visits) or to any deaths row.
rows.note: Participation (persons), the loosest exposure unit; SLSA multiplies it by visit frequency to reach the visits figure.

rows.figure: More than 13 million visitations were recorded on patrolled beaches
rows.scope: Visitations recorded on patrolled beaches in New South Wales, 1 July 2022 to 30 June 2023 (report p. 5): a count made by surf lifesaving patrols, as distinct from the survey-based coastal visitation estimate in nsw-coastal-visits-2022-23. How the counts are taken is not described in the portion read.
rows.source: Surf Life Saving New South Wales, New South Wales Coastal Safety Report 2023, p. 5
rows.do_not_add_to: Patrolled beaches during patrol hours only: not added to nsw-coastal-visits-2022-23 (which already contains these visits as the 51% share to patrolled locations), to the Australian national rows or to usla-beach-attendance-2023. Not a denominator for the same report's 48 NSW coastal drowning deaths (2022/23), which are not split by patrol status in the portion read.
rows.note: The only recorded (not surveyed) beach visit count found outside the USLA. Comparable in kind to USLA attendance but a different method and coast.

rows.figure: over 200 million individual visitations to the coast
rows.scope: SLSNSW's estimate for the 12 months to April 2023 from the National Coastal Safety Survey (online, 6-30 April 2023, national sample of 3,118 respondents aged 16 and above, run by a market research company for SLSA): 5.5 million NSW adults visited the coast, on average 3.6 times each month (males 4.1, females 3.2); 51% of visits were to patrolled locations during patrolled hours; about 2.6 hours per visit. Adults 16 and over only; any purpose.
rows.source: Surf Life Saving New South Wales, New South Wales Coastal Safety Report 2023, pp. 5 and 8 (survey method p. 43)
rows.do_not_add_to: Not added to australia-coastal-visits-2020-21 (different year; NSW is already inside the national figure) or to nsw-patrolled-beach-visits-2022-23. The report's own drowning rate is 0.59 per 100,000 population (p. 30), computed as deaths divided by population (p. 43), not per visit; its 48 coastal drowning deaths for 2022/23 (p. 5) are 85% open coronial cases (p. 43).
rows.note: Lab judgment (D): visits and deaths sit in one report for one coast and one year, so a crude risk per adult coastal visit is arithmetically possible, but the denominator counts adults on any errand while the numerator counts all ages and all coastal activities; the publisher does not compute it.

rows.figure: 4.7 million people swim twice or more a month
rows.scope: People in England who swam at least twice in the previous 28 days, Sport England Active Lives Adult Survey, 12 months to May 2019 ('May 2018/19'); the page also prints 4.9 million for November 2015-16 and 4.5 million for May 2017/18. No split between pool and open water, no age threshold stated on the page, and no trips or hours.
rows.source: Sport England, 'Swimming' research page (Active Lives Adult Survey figures), 'At a glance' and 'Active Lives' sections
rows.do_not_add_to: A participation head-count with no pool/open-water split: not a denominator for uk-waid-2024 (UK, open water, 2024) and not added to any other participation row; not current (the page's latest period is May 2018/19).
rows.note: Recorded as the only published swimming exposure measure found for the UK; the Active Lives 2023-24 data tables, which may split open-water swimming, were not opened. Lab judgment (D): no risk per swim can be formed from this.

notes: Status done: published exposure measures exist, and two publishers already divide deaths by them. (1) US boating: the Coast Guard's 2018 National Recreational Boating Safety Survey (two RTI International reports, 30 Nov 2020; release 7 Dec 2020) gives 84.5 million boaters, 17.5 boating days per boater (median 8.0) and 3.42 billion boat-hours for all recreational boats; the 2012 survey gave 3.6 billion person-hours. The Exposure report's Section 1.2 prints 2011 state fatality rates of 3 to 130 per 100 million exposure hours, and Section 3.22 (pp. 91-109) holds 2018 state risk ratios per 100 million boat days and per million boat hours (the errata corrects the Maine entry to 56 and 10). The fetch tool's PDF text stopped at p. 18, so the national boat-day and person-hour tables and Section 3.22 were not read; the 3.42 billion rests on the Coast Guard's own release and should be confirmed in Table 3-36 by eye. Compatibility: the deaths series (uscg-boating-2024, us-location-boating-2024) and the NRBSS both cover recreational vessels nationwide, so a risk per boat-hour is computable for a matching year (2018 deaths are not in the ledger); the Coast Guard has done this itself. The next survey is 2026 (NORC), no results yet. (2) US beaches: USLA attendance is estimated by each reporting agency (typically more than 140) and summed by USLA; 2023 as of 4 Nov 2023: 292,660,201 attendance, 64,578 rescues, 16 guarded and 104 unguarded drownings. Numerator and denominator come from the same agencies, beaches and year, which is why USLA's 1 in 18 million (usla-guarded-risk, still printed) is the one per-visit drowning risk in the ledger. Caveats: estimation method unstated, partial-year snapshot, non-reporting beaches excluded, and Brewster et al. 2019 say the dataset cannot be shown to be proportional exposure per visitor. The per-year database (arc.usla.org) blocks automated fetching. (3) Australia: SLSA's annual National Coastal Safety Survey (adults 16+) gives 14.4 million coastal visitors, 3.3 visits a month, 2.3 hours a visit and 'over 500 million' visits for 2020/21 (NCSR 2021, read from a mirror PDF; the 2024 and 2025 editions are Issuu-only). SLS NSW 2022/23: 13 million visits recorded on patrolled beaches, plus 5.5 million adults and 'over 200 million' visits from the survey, 51% to patrolled locations in patrol hours. Compatibility: visits are adults, any purpose, with or without water entry; coastal drowning deaths are all ages and all activities (154 for 2024/25 in australia-location-2024-25; 48 in NSW 2022/23, 85% open cases). Both publishers compute rates per 100,000 population only. Judgment (D): a crude risk per adult coastal visit is arithmetically possible from one report but mixes definitions; not computed. (4) England: Sport England's swimming page prints 4.7 million people swimming twice or more a month (May 2018/19), no pool/open-water split; no risk per swim can be formed. (5) Not found: harbour, marina or ramp launch counts; inland-water exposure anywhere; RNLI beach-visit totals (RNLI counts visitors but publishes none); a current SLSA national figure; a current Active Lives swimming figure. Grades: A for the producers' own documents, including the Coast Guard bulletin (its own release) and the SLSA 2021 PDF read from a mirror; a reviewer may prefer C for the bulletin.
